edition.name: Migne PL 3 (1844), Epistola Firmiliani ad Cyprianum, via Corpus Corporum / Latin Wikisource
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Volo autem vobis et de historia quae apud nos facta est exponere ad hoc ipsum pertinente. Ante viginti enim et duos fere annos, temporibus post Alexandrum imperatorem, multae istic conflictationes et pressurae acciderunt, vel in commune omnibus hominibus, vel privatim Christianis, terrae etiam motus plurimi et frequentes exstiterunt, ut et per Cappadociam et per Pontum multa subruerent, quaedam etiam civitates, in profundum receptae, dirupti soli hiatu devorarentur, ut ex hoc persecutio quoque gravis adversum nos christiani nominis fieret, quae post longam retro aetatis pacem repente oborta de inopinato et insueto malo ad turbandum populum nostrum terribilior effecta est. Serenianus tunc fuit in nostra provincia praeses, acerbus et dirus persecutor. In hac autem perturbatione constitutis fidelibus, et huc atque illuc persecutionis metu fugientibus, et patrias suas relinquentibus, atque in alias partes regionum transeuntibus (erat enim transeundi facultas, eo quod persecutio illa, non per totum mundum, sed localis fuisset), emersit istic subito quaedam mulier, quae in extasim constituta propheten se praeferret et quasi sancto Spiritu plena sic ageret. Ita autem principalium daemoniorum impetu ferebatur, ut per longum tempus sollicitaret et deciperet fraternitatem, admirabilia quaedam et portentosa perficiens, et facere se terram moveri polliceretur. Non quod daemoni tanta esset potestas ut terram movere aut elementum concutere vi sua valeret, sed quod nonnumquam Spiritus nequam, praesciens et intelligens terrae motum futurum, id se facturum esse simularet quod futurum videret. Quibus mendaciis et jactationibus subegerat mentes singulorum ut sibi obedirent, et quocumque praeciperet et duceret sequerentur, faceret quoque mulierem illam cruda hyeme nudis pedibus per asperas nives ire nec vexari in aliquo aut laedi illa discursione, diceret etiam se in Judaeam et Hierosolymam festinare, fingens tamquam inde venisset. Hic et unum de presbyteris Rusticum, item et alium diaconum fefellit, ut eidem mulieri commiscerentur; quod paulo post detectum est: Nam subito apparuit illi unus de exorcistis vir probatus et circa religiosam disciplinam bene semper conversatus, qui exhortatione quoque fratrum plurimorum, qui et ipsi fortes ac laudabiles in fide aderant, excitatus, erexit se contra illum spiritum nequam revincendum; qui subtili fallacia etiam hoc paulo ante praedixerat, venturum quemdam adversum et tentatorem infidelem. Tamen ille exorcista, inspiratus, Dei gratia fortiter restitit, et esse illum nequissimum spiritum qui prius sanctus putabatur, ostendit. Atque illa mulier quae prius per praestigias et fallacias daemonis multa ad deceptionem fidelium moliebatur, inter caetera quibus plurimos deceperat, etiam hoc frequenter ausa est, ut et invocatione non contemptibili sanctificare se panem et Eucharistiam facere simularet, et sacrificium Domino sine sacramento solitae praedicationis offerret, baptizaret quoque multos usitata et legitima verba interrogationis usurpans, ut nil discrepare ab ecclesiastica regula videretur.
pass_a_gloss: I want to explain to you also the story that happened among us, pertaining to this very thing. For about twenty-two years ago, in the times after Emperor Alexander, many conflicts and pressures occurred, either in common to all people or privately to Christians, and many earthquakes and frequent ones existed, so that through Cappadocia and through Pontus many things were overthrown, and certain cities, having been swallowed up into the depths, were devoured by the gaping earth, so that from this also a severe persecution against us of the Christian name was made, which after a long peace of the past age suddenly arose from an unexpected and unusual evil to disturb our people, made more terrifying. Serenianus was then the governor in our province, a harsh and dire persecutor. In this disturbance, with the faithful established and fleeing here and there in fear of persecution and leaving their homelands and crossing into other parts of the regions (for there was the ability to cross, because that persecution was not throughout the whole world but local), a certain woman suddenly emerged, who, having been placed in ecstasy, presented herself as a prophet and acted as if filled with the Holy Spirit. She was carried away by the impulse of principal demons, so that for a long time she disturbed and deceived the brotherhood, performing certain admirable and portentous things, and promising that she would make the earth move. Not that the demon had such power that it could move the earth or shake an element by its own force, but that sometimes the evil Spirit, foreseeing and understanding the future earthquake, simulated that it would do what it saw was going to happen. By these lies and boasts, she subjugated the minds of individuals so that they would obey her, and wherever she commanded and led, they would follow, and she also went with bare feet through harsh snows in the raw winter without being disturbed or harmed in any way by that walking, and she also said that she was hastening to Judea and Jerusalem, pretending as if she had come from there. Here she also deceived one of the presbyters, Rusticus, and another deacon, so that they commingled with her; which was discovered a little later: For suddenly one of the exorcists, a proven man who had always been well-conversant in religious discipline, appeared to her, who, having been exhorted also by the brothers, many of whom were strong and praiseworthy in faith, was stirred up and rose up against that evil spirit to overcome it; who, with subtle deceit, had also predicted a little before that a certain adversary and tempter of the faithless would come. Nevertheless, that exorcist, inspired by God's grace, strongly withstood, and showed that it was a most evil spirit which had previously been thought holy. And that woman, who previously, through the demon's tricks and deceptions, had undertaken many things for the deception of the faithful, among other things by which she had deceived many, also frequently dared to sanctify bread and simulate the Eucharist by not contemptible invocation, and to offer sacrifice to the Lord without the sacrament of usual preaching, and to baptize many, using the usual and legitimate words of interrogation, so that nothing seemed to differ from the ecclesiastical rule.

pass_b_english:
I also want to tell you the story of what happened among us, because it bears directly on this matter. About twenty-two years ago, after the reign of Emperor Alexander, our province suffered wave after wave of violence and oppression. Some of it fell on everyone; some was aimed specifically at Christians. Earthquakes struck again and again, toppling buildings across Cappadocia and Pontus, and in places the ground split open and swallowed entire cities. Out of that chaos a severe persecution rose against us who bear the name of Christ. It erupted suddenly after a long period of peace, an unexpected and unfamiliar evil that terrified our people more than anything before. Serenianus was governor at the time, a harsh and relentless persecutor.

Amid the turmoil the faithful stood firm, though many fled in fear, abandoned their homes, and escaped to other regions. They could do so because the persecution was local, not empire-wide. In the middle of this upheaval a woman suddenly appeared. She claimed to be in an ecstatic trance, presented herself as a prophetess, and acted as though she were filled with the Holy Spirit. In reality she was driven by the impulse of chief demons. For a long time she unsettled and deceived the brotherhood, performing astonishing and ominous signs and even promising to make the earth move. The demon did not actually have power to shake the earth or any element by its own force. Rather, the evil spirit sometimes foresees a coming quake, understands it, and then pretends it will cause what it already knows is going to happen. Through these lies and boasts she enslaved minds, so that individuals obeyed her and followed wherever she commanded and led. She walked barefoot through bitter winter snows across rough terrain without harm or distress. She also declared she was hurrying to Judea and Jerusalem, pretending she had come from there.

She deceived one of our presbyters, Rusticus, and a deacon as well, so that they had sexual relations with her. The truth came out not long afterward. One of our exorcists — a proven man who had always lived faithfully under religious discipline — suddenly confronted her. He had been urged on by many brothers, themselves strong and commendable in the faith. Stirred by their exhortation, he stood up against that evil spirit to overcome it. The spirit had tried to outwit him in advance, predicting through subtle deceit that an adversary and tempter of the faithless would come. Yet the exorcist, inspired by God's grace, resisted firmly and exposed the spirit as utterly wicked, though it had previously been thought holy.

This woman, who had already used the demon's tricks and deceptions to devise many schemes for deceiving the faithful, also repeatedly dared to sanctify bread by a solemn invocation and simulate the Eucharist, to offer sacrifice to the Lord without the sacrament of the accustomed preaching, and to baptize many using the usual and legitimate words of interrogation, so that nothing appeared to differ from the church's rule.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A is a faithful literal translation, and Pass B is a fluent rendering that preserves all nuances, including the specific meaning of 'commiscerentur' (translated as 'had sexual relations with her' in B, which is the correct sense of the Latin verb in this context, whereas A's 'commingled' is slightly more ambiguous but acceptable). All clauses, agency, and theological distinctions regarding the demon's power are preserved.
